analysis.one_liner: Replaces income, payroll, and estate taxes with a 23% national sales tax on almost everything you buy.
analysis.headline: The bill went nowhere: introduced by Senator Chambliss and four Republican cosponsors on March 29, 2007, it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a hearing or vote when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would throw out the federal income tax, the Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift tax, and replace them with a 23% national sales tax on nearly everything people buy, collected mostly by state governments for a fee. A monthly rebate would cover the tax on poverty-level spending so no one pays the tax on bare necessities. It would also stop funding the IRS after 2011. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it died when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The biggest gainers would be high-income households and people living off accumulated wealth: their investment purchases would be exempt, their income would no longer be taxed at all, and their estates would pass without estate or gift tax. Everyone would gain the convenience of never filing a federal income tax return, and every registered family would get a monthly rebate covering the tax on poverty-level spending. Businesses would buy their inputs tax-free.

how_it_helps.text: It eliminates the income tax and payroll withholding, so no one would file a federal income tax return or have tax withheld from paychecks.
Every registered family would receive a monthly rebate covering the sales tax on poverty-level spending for the family's size, paid by the Social Security Administration.
Purchases of property and services for business, investment, or export purposes would be exempt from the tax, and used goods would not be taxed again.
The IRS would stop being funded after fiscal year 2011, replaced by an Excise Tax Bureau and a Sales Tax Bureau, with states collecting the tax for a fee.

analysis.who_pays: Households that spend most or all of what they earn — the typical wage earner — would pay 23 cents in tax on nearly every dollar spent, including on new homes, cars, and services like health care beyond poverty-level amounts. People who already own wealth could spend past savings on used property without tax, and investments would be untaxed, so the burden would fall mainly on spending rather than on wealth. Families that failed to register annually would also lose their rebate payments.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wage earners who spend what they earn

drawbacks.text: The new tax would fall on consumption, so households that spend most of what they earn would pay the 23% rate on nearly every dollar they spend, while households that live off accumulated wealth or investment would owe little or nothing on their gains; the prebate only rebates the tax on poverty-level spending.

Every family would have to register annually with the tax authority, listing Social Security numbers and certifying residency, to keep receiving the monthly rebate, and a family that missed the 30-day window would stop receiving payments until it cured the lapse.

Repealing the estate and gift tax along with the income tax means the largest inheritances would pass entirely untaxed, and the bill's finding that the 16th Amendment should be repealed signals an intent to bar an income tax permanently.

Funding the government through a single consumption tax is untested at this scale; the stated 23% rate (14.91% for general revenue plus the Social Security and Medicare rates) would need to actually raise what the repealed taxes raised, and if it fell short the rate would adjust upward.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The real benefit is the end of income tax filing and the prebate that shields poverty-level spending, and some economists have argued a pure consumption tax would encourage saving. But the costs are large and land on the same people the prebate tries to protect: wage earners would pay the 23% tax on nearly every dollar they spend, while accumulated wealth and investment gains would stop being taxed at all and large estates would pass free of tax. The transition adds risk: nobody knows exactly how prices and wages would adjust when the tax switch flipped, and independent analyses have generally concluded a higher rate than 23% would be needed to replace the revenue being repealed. On balance, the bill traded a progressive tax system for a consumption tax whose burden falls hardest on people who must spend what they earn — and it was never even debated in committee, so no one bore those costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; when the 110th Congress ended, the bill died.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on March 29, 2007 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Finance.
The action history shows no further action of any kind: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote.
The bill drew four cosponsors, all Republicans.
Because the bill never advanced, the income tax, payroll taxes, estate tax, IRS, and the current tax code all remained in place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Working people are better off, because the tax burden was never shifted from wealth onto consumption: the current income tax, with its graduated rates and estate tax, kept applying to high earners and large estates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Working people, who kept the current tax system

for.name: Saxby Chambliss
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 29, 2007 and brought it to the Senate floor for introduction.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote in the Finance Committee during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the referred bill without any recorded action for the remainder of the 110th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All five Senate sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-controlled Finance Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill repeals the income, payroll, estate, and gift taxes and exempts investment purchases, so the people who owe the most under current law — those with large incomes, large portfolios, and large estates — would stop paying those taxes entirely. Ordinary people would owe the same 23% on what they buy.

States that enter cooperative agreements would collect the federal tax and keep a 0.25% administration fee, gaining a permanent paid role in federal tax collection. Because their fee is a percentage of collections, their interest runs with the tax's success rather than with keeping it low for consumers.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax advisory services
industries.note: The industry built around filing income tax returns — paid preparers, tax software, and estate planning for wealth transfer — would lose its customer base once income and estate taxes are repealed. That loss would come as a genuine reduction in filing burden for ordinary households, not just for the wealthy.

Retailers would collect and remit the tax on everything they sell and face registration, segregated accounts, bonding for large sellers, and penalties for failures; in return they would receive an administrative credit of the greater of $200 or 0.25% of tax remitted, capped at 20% of the tax due. The compliance load is new, but the credit pays for some of it.

The bill taxes fees for financial intermediation services, so banks and investment firms would owe tax on what they charge customers, but investment income and purchases held for investment would be exempt, and their wealthy clients would owe nothing on gains. Consumers would pay a new tax on the fees embedded in financial products.
